text: A building might run every device — servers, workstations, guest Wi-Fi, IoT devices — over one set of switches and cabling. Without further configuration, they all share the same broadcast domain, where broadcast traffic from any device reaches every other device, and often devices can reach each other directly too. A VLAN, or virtual LAN, solves this by letting an administrator logically split one physical network into separate broadcast domains through switch configuration alone, with no extra cabling needed.

Devices assigned to VLAN 10 behave as if they're on an entirely different network from devices on VLAN 20, even when every one of them is plugged into the exact same physical switch. For this to work across multiple switches, each switch needs a way to mark which VLAN each frame belongs to as it crosses a shared trunk link — which is exactly what 802.1Q tagging does, inserting a small tag into the Ethernet frame identifying its VLAN.

A single trunk cable connects two switches, carrying traffic for both VLAN 10 servers and VLAN 20 workstations. As a frame from a VLAN 10 device crosses that trunk, it's tagged as VLAN 10; the receiving switch reads the tag and delivers it only to other VLAN 10 ports, never to VLAN 20, even though both VLANs physically share the same cable.

VLANs are the mechanism; segmentation strategy is the decision about how to group devices. The common real-world pattern separates servers, workstations, guest Wi-Fi, and IoT devices into their own segments by role and risk. A guest on guest Wi-Fi has no legitimate reason to reach the internal file server, and a compromised IoT device, often shipped with weak default credentials and rarely updated, shouldn't be able to reach workstations or servers just because it shares the same building's network.

By keeping those groups in separate VLANs with firewall rules controlling what little traffic crosses between them, a compromise that starts in one segment doesn't automatically spread into every other segment. Up next in Chapter 2: IDS vs. IPS, moving from keeping segments apart to actively watching what moves between them.
